doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Sonny Rollins versus Coltrane, and family listening
summary: LaLama explains why he followed Rollins when others followed Coltrane, and recalls his father's records, his singer mother and James Brown.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, because that’s my influence. I mean you know I remember when I was growing up, I mean like jazz growing up let’s put it that way, it was in the 70s and everybody started playing like Coltrane. And I like Coltrane, I mean he’s one of my influences too, and Joe Henderson and those guys. But I was always towards the Sonny thing. And then moving to New York, I was different. Because I was trying to play like Sonny and everybody else was going Trane, you know? I don’t know, it probably helped me a little bit and hindered me a little bit. You know, because if they wanted the status quo they wouldn’t hire me, if they wanted something a little different they would hire me.
And I didn’t do that for any business reason. I just was turned on by it.
Well what, at the time, can you put into words what was the different approach, if you were more into Sonny than Trane? Less notes?

Less notes, more melody, more rhythm. I mean not that Trane didn’t play with rhythm, I don’t want to be quoted as saying that. But Sonny had a spontaneity. A melodic and rhythmic spontaneity I think compared to — Trane was more practiced. And even though, I mean it worked, you know don’t get me wrong, it’s not a put down by any means. It’s just what I was attracted to. It’s what I went towards. It’s what I like. You know you’ve got to be honest with yourself. And back in Youngstown prior to that, it’s what my father used to listen to. He used to listen to Sonny Stitt, Gene Ammons, Stan Getz. I mean I didn’t even hear Sonny Rollins and Trane at first, or even Charlie [Parker] until I met Tony. It wasn’t in the air in my house. I heart Stitt, singers, my mother was a singer, my father was a drummer. So I had music in the house, it was in the air, that’s the way I would put it. I like James Brown. You know, because you’re a kid. You know, not that I didn’t like jazz, I did. But James Brown, when you’re growing up, I mean that’s my generation. James Brown, the Temptations, you know.
And you got your rhythmic dose from that.
That’s right. Totally. From James, oh definitely. No doubt about it.
